_about.what: The wider world, attached to a grand campaign when it opens (src/campaign/world.ts). The history campaigns never see any of it: they keep the map of Europe. The provinces and seas themselves come from tools/build-geo-world.mjs (data/campaign/world.mjs, world-seas.json); this file holds what the rules add to them.
_about.nations: Countries that exist only on the wider map, in the same form as nations.json. Canada, Mexico and Cuba came with North America (Version 74); the six larger countries of South America, which a player can take, and the twelve small republics of Central America, the Caribbean and South America came with the Latin slice (Version 76). The small republics share one muted colour until the art director sends each its own.
_about.home: What changes for a country of nations.json once its homeland is on the map. The United States is no longer a country beyond the map's edge that wakes in December 1941: it is there from the first day, neutral, with its factories on its own soil.
_about.dominions: A mother country may stand by each of her dominions ('of'), one way only (ruling 211(b) as Brian changed it on 17 November 2026): when a country at peace with her makes war on a dominion, while the two stand in the same alliance, she answers as far as her own war in Europe allows (ruling 222, Brian's ask of 17 November 2026): 'steps' are the shares for the four steps, counting from the bottom the first that holds: 4, in danger at home (an enemy army on her home ground, or 'willGone' of her will to fight gone), two times in ten; 3, at war with one of the great powers of Europe ('europe') with her ally 'beside' not fighting beside her, four; 2, at war there with that ally fighting beside her, six; 1, no such war, eight. 'answers' is the share for a mother country with no steps. 'since' is the year each became a dominion, said on the declare card's row for the mother country (display only). One roll for each such war, made when it is declared, at the step of that day; the same at every stop of the dial and at every difficulty. A war a dominion starts is not hers. Ireland is outside. Countries not on the map yet are passed over.
_about.follow: Dominions: each goes to war with whoever its mother country is at war with on the day the world is attached.
_about.corps: The armies standing at home on the first day: [nation, name, kind, divisions, province, options]. 'str' is the strength it starts at (a peacetime army is a cadre).
_about.fleets: Fleets in home waters on the first day, in the form of navy.json.
_about.peace: The share of a great power's industry on war work while it is at peace, by month: [from month, share]. It stands in place of production.json's peaceIncome for that country.
_about.parts: The parts of the world. A League is a pact of neighbours: a founder or a member may ask only countries of its own part (the design director's ruling 58). Every country under 'nations' here lies in the part named by 'new' unless 'of' names another; every country of the old chart lies in 'europe' unless 'of' names another. Each new slice of the map adds its part.
_about.warWork: Going to war does not turn such a country's factories over in a day. From the month it is at war the share climbs from where the peace table stands by this much a month until it is all on war work (for the United States 0.037: at war in December 1941 with 35 in 100, full in June 1943; at war in September 1939 with 10 in 100, full in October 1941). It is the same for a player and for the computer. A country without a figure here works at full stretch from the day it is at war, as every other does. Canada climbs 0.022 a month from 45 in 100.
_about.works: Factories of provinces on Europe's map as the wider world counts them, against one yardstick for every smaller power (about one factory for each 18 of a 1938 economy, Italy's 8 for 141; the design director's ruling of 17 November 2026, nothing raised): Sweden has 3, at Stockholm, Gothenburg and in Varmland, where Europe's map gives it 4. The history campaigns keep Europe's figures. A factory built since the war began is added on top as ever.
_about.climbFrom: A country whose climb to war work waits for a named month: until then its share stands where the peace table puts it, war or no war, and from then on it climbs by its step (Canada: 45 in 100 to June 1940, the month the fall of France turned its factories over, then full by July 1942). A campaign that opens later finds it where the calendar has it.
_about.overseas: The army sent across the ocean. A computer-run country here with no enemy at its door beyond the old chart (an invader from across the ocean ashore anywhere on its side of the water, or a hostile country across a land frontier from ground it holds, is its army's first business; a hostile country beyond the sea on its own side, such as an Axis Brazil at war with the United States, is not: Version 78) ships the corps it raises to a port of an ally who is in the same war (never an opposed landing straight across the ocean), and from that far shore they go the way every second front goes (open.json, 'descent'): into a harbour of a landing its side has already made, or across the narrow sea when the way is open. 'guard' is how many of its field corps stay at home whatever happens. 'oceans' gives each ocean the share of the country's shipping that works that run each month (a share of 0.15 with shipping for four corps carries three corps in five months, about the pace at which the United States put its army across the Atlantic); the shares are banked from month to month up to 'bank' corps, so a month in which a landing took every ship is made up later. 'risk': no corps sails to a harbour where the danger of the crossing is above this (0.1: about six men in a hundred lost), so a beachhead beyond dangerous seas is not fed from across the ocean, and when the harbours of a second front are full the corps are put down where the army is built up and go on from there. 'ahead': its staff raises corps only as far ahead of the sailings as this many months of them, on top of the guard, so shipping is the limit of the army and not the treasury. History's dated formations are not sent to such a country as well: the corps it ships take their place. A player's own America is not run by any of this: his army forms at home and shipping it is his business. Version 77: 'hop' is a higher ceiling for one kind of sailing, a corps already on the far shore going on over a narrow sea (no further than a landing can go) into a harbour its side already holds: a reinforcement and not a venture. 'fleet' names the fleets that follow the army once its first corps is across: each moves its base to the harbour where the army is built up and takes the sea off it for its beat. 'air' is how many air groups stay at home: the others are shipped across, one a month, to the nearest airfield of its side's with room. Canada ships its army the same way, on its own small scale (its two home commands stay). So does Brazil from 'from' (59: July 1944, the month its expeditionary force sailed; its one corps has a ship as soon as it is on the quay). 'most' is the size of such an expeditionary force: no more than this many of its field corps are kept across the ocean (Canada 3, about the five divisions it had overseas; Brazil 1, its one division).
_about.protector: Overseas ground beyond the old chart whose mother country falls does not go to the victor's hands across an ocean he cannot cross: it passes into the keeping of the first of these powers that is alive, lives by its ships and is at war with the victor.
_about.pairs: Trade agreements history had in 1939, added to trade.json's. The republics of Latin America trade with their neighbours, round the continent and round the Caribbean: every one of their trading houses is spoken for on the first day, so the agreements of Europe are the same with them on the map as without.
_about.order: Where the new countries stand in the order of play: after the countries of nations.json.
_about.idle: A computer-run staff whose homeland lies beyond the old chart, with no enemy at its door there (an invader from across the ocean ashore on its side of the water, or a hostile country across a land frontier), does not go on raising an army to stand on the quay: once this many of its field corps are at home it raises no more. (A country with an entry under 'overseas' that is at war and has an ally's port to ship to raises by that rule instead.) A player's own staff is not bound by it.
_about.oilHome: What a country's small wells and plants at home yield once its own oilfields are on the map, in place of resources.json's 'home'. Off the map the United States had 120 a month from a homeland nobody could reach; on it the fields of Texas, Oklahoma and California yield 100 of that, and can be taken.
_about.labels: Where a province's name is written on the map when the middle of the province will not do (the art director's ruling on the Canal Zone, whose name ran into Panama City's): 'under' centres the name under the province's own town mark, 'west' writes it to the west of that mark, ending there. Every other name sits on the middle of its province.
_about.great: Great powers beside diplomacy.json's 'majors', once their homeland is on the map: left alone when the neutrals are dealt afresh, paid a great power's political capital and trade houses, and counted among the great powers of the last act.

corps: 1st Army Division and the Campo de Mayo garrison
